sections.h2: Who values and who collects in Hopkins County?
sections.html:
The PVA in Madisonville lists and values every parcel, and the Sheriff bills and collects. The PVA keeps a roster of property and owners, photographs and measures buildings, and prepares the tax roll that the public may inspect. Its home is the Courthouse Annex, 25 East Center Street, Madisonville, KY 42431, telephone (270) 821-3092.

The Sheriff's Office is at 261 Responders Lane, phone 270-821-5661, and posts hours of 8 AM to 4 PM on weekdays. Bills that remain open after April 15 belong to the Hopkins County Clerk, reachable at 270-326-2097.

A bill follows the name on the parcel as of January 1. When you buy in spring, the former owner may still get the paper and should pass it along. The Sheriff cannot see new deeds, so a buyer without a bill can call the office or print one from its website.

sections.h2: What does the Hopkins County collection calendar look like?
sections.html:
Mailing normally happens about September 30, and the counter opens October 1. The Sheriff posts four stages through April 15.

Stages of the Hopkins County Sheriff's yearly tax collection (source: Hopkins County Sheriff's Office FAQ)
StageWhat changes
October 1 to November 12 percent discount
November 2 to December 31Face amount
January 1 to January 315 percent added
February 1 to April 1521 percent added

The Sheriff's page lists 21 percent for the last stage. KRS 134.015 sets a 10 percent penalty after January, and the Department of Revenue's explainer shows a Sheriff's add-on fee and commission as well. Phone the office for an exact payoff if you plan to pay in February or March.

State law ends the Sheriff's collection at close of business on April 15, and open bills then pass to the Clerk.

sections.h2: Which payment methods does the Hopkins County Sheriff accept?
sections.html:
The office takes online payments and counter payments, and it insists on the whole amount. A partial payment is turned down.

  • Forms taken: cash, check, money order, cashier's check and credit card.
  • A third-party processor runs card payments for 2.5 percent plus 30 cents.
  • Online checks cost $1.50 to process.
  • Write checks to Hopkins County Sheriff.

Homeowners with an escrow account still need to act. The Sheriff states that sending the bill to the mortgage servicer is the owner's job, and a servicer cannot pay a bill it never saw.

sections.h2: How do I estimate and prorate a Hopkins County bill?
sections.html:
Take the taxable assessment, divide by 100 and multiply by that year's rate. Volunteer fire department fees or watershed taxes, where they apply, are added separately.

The Sheriff's FAQ also gives a sale formula. Divide the last year's bill by 365 for a daily cost, then multiply by the number of days the seller lived in the house. A seller who closes on June 30 owes about 181 days' worth.

Some closing agents wait for the real bill. Compare their number with the Sheriff's method before you sign the settlement statement, and ask which year's bill each of you used.

sections.h2: How do I fight a Hopkins County assessment?
sections.html:
Talk to the PVA first. KRS 133.120 requires a conference with the PVA or a deputy before or during the inspection period, and phone conferences are allowed on request.

  • The PVA explains how the value was built and keeps a written record of the conference.
  • Next, file a letter or petition with the County Clerk by one workday after the inspection period ends.
  • State the value you believe is fair and attach evidence: land and building details, insurance, construction costs, listings, sales or loan papers.
  • Attend the hearing yourself or send an authorized representative.

A board can dismiss an appeal when you withhold information it reasonably requests. Meanwhile your bill stays payable on the value you claimed.

sections.h2: Which Hopkins County owners qualify for a tax reduction?
sections.html:
Owners 65 or older, and those totally disabled, can deduct $49,100 for the 2025 and 2026 assessment years if the home is their primary residence.

On the $142,800 Census value for a typical owned home here, the deduction leaves $93,700 to be taxed. The application is completed at the PVA office with proof of age, often a birth certificate or driver's license. Disability claims need proof of payments received from January through December.

Farmland gets different treatment. The Sheriff's page cites KRS 132.010, which values agricultural land by its production capability, and describes qualifying land as ten or more acres used for livestock or crops, timber included. Nobody can claim more than one exemption on one property within one county and state.

sections.h2: What happens to a Hopkins County tax debt after the Clerk takes over?
sections.html:
The bill becomes a certificate of delinquency at the Clerk's office, and a lien is recorded on the property. Selling the house does not erase it.

The Clerk's 2025 sale gives a picture of the next step. It ran October 8, 2025, electronically, with the Clerk's office at 24 Union Street in Madisonville handling registration. Buyers paid $5 per priority bill or $10 per current-year bill, with a $250 cap on combined fees. Payment in full was due by October 10 or the purchase was void.

A buyer of a certificate can load its own fees on the account, so clearing the bill with the Sheriff before the deadline, or with the Clerk afterward, costs less. The Sheriff's website and the Clerk's website do not link, so call the Clerk for current amounts instead of trusting the Sheriff's listing.

sections.h2: What should a Madisonville-area seller know about Hopkins County?
sections.html:
Hopkins County sits in western Kentucky with Madisonville as seat and largest city. It was created on December 9, 1806 from Henderson County and has 542 square miles of land. The Pond, Tradewater and Green rivers cross it, with flat river valleys in the north and rolling hills in the south and center.

Coal mines work the southern end and farms fill the north, mostly soybeans, corn and tobacco. The Pennyrile Parkway and Western Kentucky Parkway both pass through. Other incorporated places include Dawson Springs, Earlington, Nortonville, Mortons Gap, Hanson, White Plains, Nebo and St. Charles.

  • 45,127 residents in 2025, down 0.6 percent from 2020.
  • $142,800 as the typical owned-home value (2020 to 2024).
  • 70.7 percent of homes occupied by their owners.
  • $56,815 median household income.
  • $837 median gross rent.

Hopkins County Schools covers most of the county, while Dawson Springs runs its own district.

faqs.q: What day does the Hopkins County discount period begin?
faqs.a: October 1, once bills have been mailed around September 30. The 2 percent discount ends November 1, and the face amount holds until December 31.

faqs.q: Will Hopkins County let me split a bill into pieces?
faqs.a: No. The Sheriff requires full payment. Cash, check, money order, cashier's check and cards are accepted, and cards carry a processor fee.

faqs.q: I closed last month and received no bill. Who do I call?
faqs.a: The Sheriff at 270-821-5661. Bills are addressed to whoever owned the parcel on January 1, and the Sheriff cannot see new deeds. You can also print a copy of the bill from the Sheriff's website.

faqs.q: Whom do I pay once April 15 has gone by?
faqs.a: The Hopkins County Clerk, at 270-326-2097 according to the Sheriff's page. All unpaid bills move there at the close of business on April 15.

faqs.q: Do older owners get any relief?
faqs.a: Yes, the $49,100 homestead exemption, filed at the PVA office, 25 East Center Street. It covers owners 65 or older who live in the home, and totally disabled owners qualify too.
